subject: Climate & Environment
title: What a 100% Renewable World Looks Like
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on What a 100% Renewable World Looks Like.

hook.text: Can the whole world run on sun, wind, and water? Multiple studies say yes — technically.

buildup.text: The energy is there. Earth receives more solar energy in one hour than humans use in a year.

discovery.text: A 100% renewable grid needs massive storage, upgraded transmission, and flexible demand.

twist.text: The hardest sectors are aviation, shipping, and high-heat industry — not electricity.

climax.text: The transition is less about technology and more about political will and investment speed.

punchline.text: The sun sends enough energy every hour. We just need to catch it.

quiz.question: How much solar energy does Earth receive compared to human use?
options: More in one hour than we use in a year

details.summary: A fully renewable energy system would rely on massive solar and wind deployment, complemented by storage, hydrogen, and grid interconnections spanning continents.
details.whyItMatters: Envisioning a 100 percent renewable world clarifies the scale of investment and coordination needed. It shows decarbonization is possible with existing technology if political will matches ambition.
takeaways: Studies show 100 percent renewables is technically feasible
Solar and wind would provide the bulk of generation
Massive storage and intercontinental grids are essential

faq.question: What technologies would a 100 percent renewable world need?
faq.answer: Primarily solar and wind for generation, with lithium-ion and flow batteries for short-term storage, hydrogen for seasonal storage and industry, pumped hydro, enhanced geothermal for baseload, and high-capacity intercontinental transmission lines.

faq.question: How much would a full renewable transition cost?
faq.answer: Estimates range from $60 to $100 trillion in cumulative investment through 2050. However, avoided fuel costs and health savings from ending fossil combustion largely offset this, and many studies show a net economic benefit over business as usual.
